It is clearly desirable to achieve the highest percentage yield of product possible to reduce the consumption of raw ma­te­rials. In some synthetic reactions (especially in organic chemistry), the final product is the result of many successive reactions. In such processes, the yields in the individual steps must be quite high if the syn­ thetic method is to be a practical success. Suppose, for example, that ten consecu­ tive reactions must be performed to reach the product, and that each has a percent­ age yield of only 50% (a fractional yield of 0.5). The overall yield is the product of the fractional yields of the steps:
10 terms

This overall percentage yield of 0.1% makes the process useless for synthetic pur­ poses. If all the individual percentage yields could be increased to 90%, however, the overall yield would then be (0.9)10 5 0.35, or 35%. This is a much more rea­ sonable result, and one that might make the process worth considering.
